10110:
"Long in the tooth" is an idiom that simply means old or getting old. When you say someone or something is "long in the tooth," you are saying they are aging, often with the quiet suggestion that they may be past their best days or showing the natural wear of time.

Example: "He's a bit long in the tooth to be playing professional football."
That sentence means: He is too old to still be playing professional football.

This idiom was born from the world of horses, and once you understand this, the phrase will make perfect and permanent sense in your mind.

Historically, people bought and sold horses regularly, and a horse's age was one of the most important things a buyer needed to know. An old horse cannot work as hard, run as fast, or last as long as a young one. So buyers needed a reliable way to check a horse's age — especially because dishonest sellers might lie about it.

The answer was in the horse's mouth.

As a horse ages, its gums slowly recede (pull back and shrink). Because the gums are pulling away, more and more of each tooth becomes exposed and visible. So the teeth of an older horse look longer than the teeth of a young horse — even though the teeth haven't actually grown. It's the gums that have shrunk, giving the illusion of longer teeth.

So when a knowledgeable buyer opened a horse's mouth and saw very long-looking teeth, they immediately knew: this horse is old. A young horse, on the other hand, has short-looking teeth because its gums are full and healthy, covering more of each tooth.

Over time, people started applying this horse-inspection logic to humans and other things, using it as a casual, slightly humorous way to say "old."

The short version of the origin: Old horse = long-looking teeth. Long teeth = old. "Long in the tooth" = old.

This is also why another famous idiom exists: "Don't look a gift horse in the mouth." That phrase warns you not to examine a gift too critically — because if someone gives you a horse for free, it's rude and ungrateful to immediately check its teeth (i.e., judge its age and value). Both idioms share the same historical root.

This is an important nuance to understand.

"Long in the tooth" is not a harsh insult. It sits somewhere between a neutral observation and a gentle, slightly humorous comment. It often carries a tone of mild affection or light teasing rather than cruelty.

Think of it this way — if a 60-year-old uncle tries to do a back-flip at a family party, someone might chuckle and say, "He's getting a little long in the tooth for that!" It's not mean-spirited. It's fond and a little funny.

That said, context always matters. If someone says it coldly or dismissively — "She's too long in the tooth for this job" — it can feel unkind. Use your judgment based on the situation and the speaker's tone.

You can also use it about yourself, and when you do, it usually sounds self-aware and charming:
"I'm a bit long in the tooth to be staying up until 3 AM!"
What Can Be "Long in the Tooth"?

This is one of the most flexible things about this idiom. It's not only used for people. It can describe:

People: "The professor is getting long in the tooth, but his lectures are still brilliant."

Animals: "That old dog is long in the tooth, but he still runs to the door every time I come home."

Objects (cars, machines, technology, buildings): "That laptop is getting long in the tooth — it can barely run modern software."

Organizations, ideas, or systems: "Some people think the traditional 9-to-5 workday is getting a bit long in the tooth in the modern world."

The common thread in all of these is the same: whatever is being described has been around a long time and is showing its age.

When you call something "long in the tooth," you're not just saying it's old — you're adding a quiet layer of meaning underneath. You're suggesting:

  • It has been around for a long time.
  • It may be struggling to keep up with newer, younger, or fresher things.
  • It still exists and functions, but perhaps not at its peak.

It's the difference between saying "That car is old" and "That car is getting long in the tooth." The second version paints a more vivid picture — you can almost see the old car sputtering along, a little worn, a little tired, but still going.

• "The actor is a little long in the tooth to be playing a teenage hero, but somehow it works."
  • "Our company's software is getting long in the tooth — we need to upgrade."
  • "I know I'm long in the tooth for this kind of adventure, but I still want to try."
  • "The tradition is long in the tooth, but people still love it."
  • "Even long in the tooth, she danced with more grace than anyone half her age."

MeaningOld; aging; past one's prime
OriginHorse's gums recede with age, making teeth look longer — so long teeth = old horse
ToneGently humorous, mildly affectionate; not usually harsh
Used forPeople, animals, objects, systems, ideas — anything that ages
FeelingSuggests something has been around a long time and may be struggling to keep up

The beauty of this idiom is its story. Every time you hear or use "long in the tooth," you can picture a wise old horse, mouth open, with teeth that have seen better days — and the meaning will never leave you.
10111:
"A long shot" means something that has a very small chance of succeeding. It is an attempt, a hope, or a possibility that is unlikely — but not completely impossible.

When you call something "a long shot," you are saying:

  • The odds are against it.
  • Most people would expect it to fail.
  • Success would be surprising.

But here is the key: a long shot is still worth trying. It is not zero chance — it is just a low chance.

"Winning the lottery is a long shot, but people still buy tickets."

This idiom has two likely roots, and both involve the idea of physical distance.

1. Shooting (guns or arrows):
Imagine a soldier or a hunter firing at a target that is very far away. The farther the target, the harder it is to aim accurately, and the less likely the shot is to hit. This is a "long shot" — a shot taken from a long distance, with a low chance of hitting the mark. Over time, people started using this image to describe any attempt that is unlikely to succeed.

2. Horse racing:
In horse racing, each horse is given "odds" — numbers that show how likely it is to win. A horse with very low chances of winning is called a "long shot." If you bet on that horse and it wins, you get a huge payout — but most of the time, it loses. This use of the phrase became very popular in the 19th century and helped spread the idiom into everyday English.

Both origins share the same core idea: a difficult, unlikely, but not impossible attempt.

1. As a noun (the most common use)

Here, "a long shot" is a thing — a plan, a person, or an idea that is unlikely to succeed.

"Applying to Harvard is a long shot for most students."
"He's a long shot for the presidency, but his campaign is growing."
"It's a long shot, but let's try anyway."

Notice the tone: there is hope mixed with realism. You know the chances are slim, but you're not giving up.

2. "Not by a long shot" — meaning "not at all" or "far from it"

This is one of the most common phrases built from this idiom. When you say "not by a long shot," you are strongly saying that something is far from true, far from enough, or far from the mark.

Think of it this way: imagine an arrow fired at a target. If the arrow misses "by a long shot," it doesn't just barely miss — it misses by a huge distance. So "not by a long shot" means "not even close."

"Are you finished with your homework?" — "Not by a long shot." (meaning: I've barely started)
"Is this the best pizza in the city?" — "Not by a long shot." (meaning: it is nowhere near the best)
"Did the team play well?" — "Not by a long shot." (meaning: they played very poorly)

This phrase is used to strongly disagree or deny something, often with a bit of surprise or emphasis.

3. "By a long shot" — meaning "by a great margin" or "by far"

When used in a positive statement (without "not"), it means something is clearly the best, biggest, most, or greatest — by a lot. It emphasizes a large gap or difference.

"She is the most talented student in the class, by a long shot." (she is clearly far better than everyone else)
"This is the best film of the year, by a long shot." (no other film comes close)
"He is the fastest runner on the team, by a long shot." (there is no competition)
The Emotional Flavor of "A Long Shot"

This idiom carries a particular feeling with it. It is honest and hopeful at the same time. When someone says "it's a long shot," they are:

  • Being realistic — they are not pretending the chances are high.
  • Staying brave — they are not giving up either.
  • Preparing the listener — so that if it fails, it's not a shock.

This is why you often hear it paired with phrases like "but worth trying" or "but I'll go for it."

"Getting into that film school is a long shot for me, but I'm going to apply."
"It's a long shot, but we might just pull this off."

It is the language of people who understand the odds yet decide to try anyway. There is something admirable in that.

It is important to be clear about what this phrase does not mean:

  • It does not mean impossible. If something were impossible, you would say "there's no chance" or "it's out of the question." A long shot still has some chance.
  • It does not mean easy. The opposite of a long shot is a "sure thing" or a "safe bet" — something very likely to succeed.
  • It does not mean the person is foolish for trying. In fact, people admire those who take long shots — especially when they succeed.
Real-Life Situations Where You'd Use It

• Job hunting: "Applying to that company is a long shot — they rarely hire freshers — but I'll send my résumé."
  • Sports: "Our team is a long shot to win the tournament, but stranger things have happened."
  • Exams / competitions: "Topping the national exam is a long shot, but I'm going to give it everything I have."
  • Business: "Getting that big investor on board is a long shot, but one meeting could change everything."
  • Daily life: "Will the bus arrive on time in this traffic?" — "Not by a long shot."

PhraseMeaning

"A long shot" = something unlikely to succeed, but still possible and worth attempting.

"Not by a long shot" = not at all; not even close; far from it.

"By a long shot" = by a great margin; clearly the most or best.

The idiom comes from the world of shooting and horse racing, where a shot or a horse from far away — with low odds — still had a chance. Today, it lives in everyday English to describe any situation where hope survives against the odds.

The next time you face a challenge that seems unlikely but not impossible, you'll know exactly what to call it — and exactly how to say it.
10112:
Long-winded describes someone or something that uses far more words than necessary to say something. A long-winded person takes a very long time to reach their point, often repeating themselves, going off on side topics, or building up slowly to a simple conclusion — when they could have just said it simply and briefly.

The key is the word unnecessary. It is not just "long." It is wastefully long. The extra length adds no real value. The same thing could have been said in a fraction of the time or words.

When you listen to or read something long-winded, you typically feel:

  • Bored — because nothing new is being added
  • Impatient — because you are waiting for the person to finally get to the point
  • Drained — because your time and energy feel wasted

This is what separates long-winded from simply detailed or thorough. A detailed explanation is long for a good reason — it adds clarity, depth, or useful information. A long-winded explanation is long for no good reason — it just circles around, repeats, and meanders.
Who or What Can Be Long-winded?

The adjective can describe people and things:

People — A speaker, writer, teacher, politician, or anyone who communicates.

"My uncle is so long-winded — he takes 20 minutes to tell a 2-minute story."

Spoken things — A speech, lecture, explanation, answer, or presentation.

"The CEO gave a long-winded speech that should have ended an hour earlier."

Written things — An email, essay, letter, article, or book.

"His long-winded email could have been a single sentence."

Meetings or conversations — Any interaction that drags on unnecessarily.

"The meeting was so long-winded that everyone lost focus."
The Tone — It Is Always a Criticism

Long-winded is never a compliment. It is always negative. When you call someone long-winded, you are politely (or sometimes not so politely) saying their communication is tedious, undisciplined, and inconsiderate of other people's time.

Think of it this way: a good communicator respects your time. A long-winded communicator does not — whether intentionally or not.

• "Don't ask him for directions. He's so long-winded that you'll be standing there for fifteen minutes."
  • "The judge asked the lawyer to stop being long-winded and get to the point."
  • "She wrote a long-winded apology that should have just said 'I'm sorry.'"
  • "I stopped reading that book because the author was too long-winded."
  • "His long-winded explanation just made things more confusing, not less."

These words share the spirit of long-winded, though with slight differences in shade:

  • Verbose — using too many words (more formal, used mainly in writing)
  • Wordy — same idea, very common in everyday speech
  • Rambling — talking or writing without a clear direction, going off on tangents
  • Prolix — excessively long in speech or writing (formal and literary)
  • Garrulous — excessively talkative (applies to people, not writing)
  • Drawn-out — stretched out unnecessarily over time

These describe the ideal — the opposite of long-winded:

  • Concise — expressing a lot in few words, with nothing wasted
  • Brief — short in length
  • Succinct — short, clear, and expressing exactly what needs to be said
  • To the point — getting directly to what matters
  • Pithy — brief but full of meaning and substance
A Simple Way to Remember It

Imagine someone is asked: "What time is it?"

A concise person says: "It's 3 o'clock."

A long-winded person says: "Well, you know, I checked my watch a moment ago — it's the one my grandfather gave me, actually a lovely old piece — and I believe, if I recall correctly, and accounting for the fact that I may have set it a minute or two ahead last Tuesday, it was somewhere around, give or take, approximately 3 in the afternoon, though of course that depends on your time zone..."

Same information. Vastly different amounts of words. The second version is long-winded.

Being long-winded is not always a character flaw. Some people are long-winded out of nervousness (they keep talking to fill silence), some out of enthusiasm (they love their topic too much), and some simply because they have never developed the skill of editing themselves. It is a communication habit, not necessarily a measure of intelligence or intention.

However, regardless of the cause, the effect on the listener or reader is the same — patience tested, time spent, attention lost. That is why long-winded always carries a critical, negative meaning.
10113: Longevity means the state or condition of living, existing, or lasting for a notably long time. It is the quality of being long-lasting. When you say something or someone has longevity, you are saying they have continued to exist, function, or remain relevant for a period that is significantly greater than what is typical or expected.
When it refers to people and living things

The most common use of longevity is about how long a living being — a person, an animal, or even a plant — lives. A person who lives to 98 years has remarkable longevity. Scientists who study human longevity are trying to understand why certain people live far longer than others, and what role genes, habits, diet, and environment play in that. In medicine and biology, longevity is a serious subject of research, because understanding it can help us all live healthier, longer lives.

"The people of that island are famous for their longevity — most of them live well past ninety."

In this sense, longevity is close in meaning to "long life," but it is a more formal, precise word. It does not simply mean "being old." It refers to the measurable length of a life, especially when that length is impressive or worth noting.
When it refers to things other than living beings

Longevity is also widely used for careers, products, institutions, relationships, ideas, and really anything that exists over time. If a television series has been running for twenty seasons, you would say it has impressive longevity. If a company has been in business for a century, that is longevity. If a friendship has lasted forty years through all kinds of hardship, that too is longevity.

"The longevity of her acting career is extraordinary — she has been performing for over five decades."

"This type of paint was engineered for longevity — it resists fading and cracking for many years."

"What is the secret to the longevity of their marriage?"
The tone and feeling the word carries

Longevity almost always carries a positive, admiring tone. When we describe something as having longevity, we are typically expressing respect or being impressed. It suggests not merely that something lasted a long time, but that there is something worthy of admiration in that endurance — quality, strength, value, or resilience.
How much time are we actually talking about?

Longevity does not simply mean "lasting a while." It implies a length of time that is notably and meaningfully greater than the average or expected. A car battery that lasts one extra month does not have longevity. A car that still runs perfectly after thirty years does. The word is reserved for durations that are genuinely striking.
Phrases and combinations you will commonly encounter

You will frequently see longevity paired with certain words. People speak of the "secrets of longevity" when discussing what makes someone live long. "Career longevity" refers to sustaining a profession over many years. "Human longevity" is used in scientific and medical contexts. You will also hear phrases like "remarkable longevity," "extraordinary longevity," "promote longevity," and "achieve longevity." These combinations are natural and very common.
How longevity differs from similar words

It helps to know how longevity compares to words that seem related. Longevity and endurance are different because endurance suggests actively struggling or pushing through hardship, while longevity simply means lasting a long time, without necessarily implying any struggle at all. Longevity and immortality are also different — immortality means living forever with no end, whereas longevity still has limits, just very generous ones. Finally, longevity and durability overlap somewhat, but durability is usually reserved for physical objects and emphasizes their ability to resist wear and damage. Longevity is broader and more flexible — it applies equally well to a human life, a business, a piece of music, a political idea, or a brand of jeans.

Longevity, as a noun, means the state of living or lasting for a notably long time. It applies to people, animals, careers, relationships, products, and ideas. It carries a positive, admiring tone. It implies a length of time that is genuinely impressive, not just slightly above average. And it is a versatile word that fits naturally into conversations about health, history, business, culture, and everyday life.
10114:
Longing is a deep, persistent feeling of wanting something or someone that you do not have — and often cannot easily have, or cannot have at all. It is not just a casual wish. It carries an emotional ache — a feeling that something important is missing from your life, and that its absence hurts.

Think of it this way: when you want a glass of water, that is a simple, neutral desire. You get it, the want disappears. But longing is different. It stays. It lingers. It sits quietly in your chest like a dull, persistent pain that does not go away.

The heart of longing is distance — a gap between you and what you deeply wish for. That gap can be:

  • Physical distance — a person you love is far away, and you ache to be with them.
  • Time distance — the thing you long for is in the past, and you cannot go back. You long for a simpler time in your childhood, for example.
  • Impossibility — sometimes what you long for can never be yours at all, which makes the feeling even sharper.

There is always a sense of helplessness mixed into longing. You are not taking action to get what you want. You are just feeling the absence of it, deeply.

It is a sustained feeling, not a brief flash. You do not "long" for something for a single second and forget it. Longing tends to return, quietly, again and again.

Longing is one of those rare emotions that is painful and precious at the same time. It hurts — yes — but it also connects you to what you love. A person who longs for a late parent is still holding that love alive inside them. A person who longs for a home they left behind is honoring the beauty that place held for them. Because of this, longing often has a bittersweet quality — sad, but also meaningful.

• Missing a person who has passed away, moved far away, or drifted out of your life
  • Missing your childhood, or a happier time in your past (this specific kind is often called nostalgia, which is essentially longing for the past)
  • Wishing you could live somewhere else, or return to a place you loved (homesickness is longing for home specifically)
  • Carrying an unfulfilled dream or aspiration — you long for a life you did not live
  • Longing to be loved, understood, or accepted

• "She felt a deep longing for her hometown every time it rained."
  • "He was overcome by a sudden longing to hear his mother's voice."
  • "There was a quiet longing in her heart for things that could never be."
  • "The old photograph stirred a longing in him he had almost forgotten."
  • "She tried to suppress the longing, but it returned every evening."

Notice how the word "longing" in each sentence conveys not just want, but weight — there is something tender and aching about each one.
How Longing Differs from Similar Words

These words are in the same emotional family, but each has its own flavor:

Desire — A strong wish, often for something you could realistically pursue. It is more neutral and active. Desire can lead to action; longing often just sits with you.

Yearning — The closest word to longing, and often used interchangeably. However, yearning tends to feel slightly more urgent and fervent — as if the feeling is pushing outward. Longing can be quieter, more subdued and inward.

Wistfulness — A softer, gentler cousin of longing. Wistfulness is tinged with mild, dreamy sadness. It is what you feel when you see an old photograph and smile sadly. Longing is deeper and heavier than wistfulness.

Craving — More physical, more urgent, more about an immediate need (craving food, craving sleep). It does not carry the emotional depth or the sense of distance that longing does.

Pining — Longing for a specific person, often romantically, often while waiting. Pining has a patient, quietly suffering quality. If longing is the emotion, pining is what it looks like over time.

Nostalgia — Longing specifically for the past — a time, a place, a version of life. Nostalgia is a specific type of longing.

Homesickness — Longing specifically for home. Again, a subset of longing.

So longing is the broad, deep umbrella under which many of these others fall.

Longing sits in the middle-to-deep range of emotional intensity. It is stronger than a casual wish or mild preference. But unlike craving or desperation, it does not always make you act. It is possible to live with longing for years — quietly, persistently — without it ever being fully resolved.

Sometimes it fades. Sometimes it never does.

Longing is a deep, lingering ache for something or someone you do not have — often something beyond easy reach — that stays with you, quietly but persistently, and makes you feel the weight of what is missing.
10115:
Imagine holding a globe of the Earth. Now imagine slicing it like an orange — not across the middle, but from the top (North Pole) to the bottom (South Pole). Each slice you make would be a thin, wedge-shaped section of the Earth. The curved edge on the surface of each such slice — a line running from the North Pole straight down to the South Pole — is called a line of longitude, or a meridian.

Longitude is a way of measuring how far east or west a particular location on Earth is, using these imaginary lines as a reference system.
Why Do We Need It?

The Earth is a sphere. To describe the exact position of any point on a sphere, you need two pieces of information — just like how to describe a point on a flat grid you need both an X value and a Y value. For Earth:

  • Latitude tells you how far north or south you are.
  • Longitude tells you how far east or west you are.

Together, latitude and longitude form a coordinate system that can pinpoint any location on Earth with complete precision.
The Starting Line: The Prime Meridian

To measure "how far east or west," you need a starting point — a reference line to measure from. That line is called the Prime Meridian, and it is assigned a longitude of 0° (zero degrees).

The Prime Meridian is an internationally agreed-upon imaginary line that runs from the North Pole to the South Pole, passing through Greenwich, a town in London, England. This choice was made historically (in 1884) and has been used worldwide ever since.

Everything to the east of this line is called East longitude, and everything to the west is called West longitude.
How Longitude Is Measured

Longitude is measured in degrees (°), using the center of the Earth as the point from which the angle is calculated.

Think of it this way: if you stood at the center of the Earth and looked outward, the angle between the Prime Meridian (0°) and the line going to your chosen location on the surface — measured either eastward or westward — is that location's longitude.

  • The Prime Meridian itself is 0° longitude.
  • Moving eastward from it, longitude increases from 0° to 180° East.
  • Moving westward from it, longitude increases from 0° to 180° West.
  • The 180° line (called the International Date Line, roughly) is on the exact opposite side of the Earth from the Prime Meridian. Going east or going west, you meet it at the same line — so 180° East and 180° West are the same line.

This means the full range of longitude values is: 180° West → 0° → 180° East, covering the entire Earth.
How Degrees Are Further Divided

Because degrees are large units, longitude can also be expressed in smaller units for greater precision:

  • Each degree (°) is divided into 60 minutes (′)
  • Each minute is divided into 60 seconds (″)

So a longitude might be written as: 73° 56′ 18″ E — meaning 73 degrees, 56 minutes, and 18 seconds east of the Prime Meridian. This level of precision can pin a location to within a few meters on the Earth's surface.

In modern GPS systems, the minutes and seconds are often replaced with decimal degrees instead — e.g., 73.938° E — which means the same thing but is easier for computers to work with.
What Lines of Longitude Look Like

All lines of longitude are:

  • Equal in length — every meridian runs from the North Pole to the South Pole, so they are all the same length (unlike lines of latitude, which shrink as you go toward the poles).
  • Shaped like half-circles — each one is a semicircle on the globe's surface.
  • Converging at the poles — all lines of longitude meet at both the North Pole and the South Pole, like the segments of an orange meeting at the top and bottom.
  • Farthest apart at the Equator — the distance between two neighboring lines of longitude is widest at the Equator and shrinks to zero at the poles.
Reading a Longitude Value

When you see a longitude value, here's how to read it:

  • 0° → You're on the Prime Meridian (through London).
  • 90° E → You're one-quarter of the way around the Earth going east (roughly near Bangladesh/Bhutan).
  • 90° W → You're one-quarter of the way around going west (roughly through the central United States).
  • 180° → You're on the opposite side of the Earth from the Prime Meridian (in the middle of the Pacific Ocean).

For reference, India sits roughly between 68° E and 97° E longitude, which is why your clocks are ahead of London by 5 hours and 30 minutes.
Longitude and Time Zones

This brings up one of the most practical uses of longitude: time zones.

The Earth takes 24 hours to rotate 360°. So it rotates:

360° ÷ 24 hours = 15° per hour

This means every 15° of longitude you move east, the local time is one hour ahead, and every 15° you move west, it is one hour behind.

This is why time zones exist and why they follow longitude lines roughly. For example, India Standard Time (IST) is UTC+5:30 because India is approximately 82.5° East of the Prime Meridian (82.5 ÷ 15 = 5.5 hours = 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of Greenwich).
Longitude vs. Latitude — A Quick Contrast

These two are often confused, so here's the clearest way to tell them apart:

LongitudeLatitude
Direction measuredEast–WestNorth–South
Lines runNorth–South (top to bottom)East–West (side to side)
Range0° to 180° E or W0° to 90° N or S
All lines equal length?YesNo
Lines meet?Yes, at the polesNo, they are parallel

A helpful memory trick: "Lat" is flat — lines of latitude are horizontal (flat) bands wrapping around the Earth like rings. Lines of longitude, on the other hand, are long — they run the full length of the Earth from pole to pole.
Real-World Uses of Longitude

Longitude is not just an academic concept — it is used everywhere:

  • Navigation: Ships, aircraft, and GPS devices use longitude (together with latitude) to determine their exact position anywhere on Earth.
  • Mapping: Every map and atlas uses a grid of latitude and longitude lines to locate places accurately.
  • Time zones: As explained, the world's time zones are built directly on the concept of longitude.
  • Satellite systems: Satellites in geostationary orbit (like communication and weather satellites) are positioned and identified by their longitude above the Equator.
  • Surveying and construction: Large-scale engineering projects use longitude to establish precise locations.
  • Astronomy: Longitude is also adapted for use in celestial coordinate systems to locate objects in the sky.
Summary

Longitude is a measurement that tells you how far east or west a point on Earth is from the Prime Meridian — an imaginary reference line running from pole to pole through Greenwich, England. It is expressed in degrees, ranging from 0° at the Prime Meridian to 180° in either direction. Lines of longitude run vertically from pole to pole, and all of them meet at the poles. Together with latitude, longitude gives every location on Earth a unique, precise address. It also forms the mathematical basis for the world's time zones.
10116:
Longstanding describes something that has existed, continued, or been in place for a long time — and is still going on or still relevant right now (or at the time being spoken about).

The two key ideas packed into this single word are:

  • Long duration — it started a long time ago.
  • Continuity — it has kept going without stopping in a major way.

If something is longstanding, it is not new, not recent, and not temporary. It has a history behind it and is still present.
A Simple Way to Picture It

Imagine a river that has been flowing through a valley for hundreds of years. It didn't just appear yesterday. It has been there, flowing continuously, for a very long time. You could call it a longstanding feature of that landscape.

Now replace the river with a friendship, a problem, a rule, a tradition, or a disagreement — the idea is the same. Something began long ago and has kept going.
What Kinds of Things Can Be "Longstanding"?

This word is very flexible. It can describe many kinds of things, both positive and negative:

Relationships and connections

  • A longstanding friendship — two people who have been close friends for many years.
  • A longstanding alliance — two countries that have been partners for a long time.
  • A longstanding rivalry — two teams or people who have been competing against each other for years.

Problems and disputes

  • A longstanding problem — an issue that has existed for a long time and hasn't been solved.
  • A longstanding dispute — a disagreement or conflict between two parties that has continued for years.
  • A longstanding feud — a bitter, ongoing conflict between families or groups that has lasted a long time.

Traditions, beliefs, and practices

  • A longstanding tradition — something people have been doing for a long time and continue to do.
  • A longstanding belief — an idea or conviction that a person or group has held for many years.
  • A longstanding custom — a way of doing things that has been practiced for a long time.

Policies, agreements, and rules

  • A longstanding policy — a rule or approach that an organization has followed for a long time.
  • A longstanding agreement — a deal or understanding between two parties that has been in place for years.

As you can see, "longstanding" does not judge whether the thing is good or bad. A longstanding friendship is wonderful; a longstanding problem is frustrating. The word simply tells you about time and continuity — nothing more.

One important thing to understand is that "longstanding" does not mean a fixed amount of time. It is always relative to the context.

  • In a company that was started last year, a policy from six months ago might already be called longstanding.
  • In a country with a thousand-year history, a tradition from two hundred years ago is longstanding.
  • In a person's life, a habit they've had for ten years could be called longstanding.

The point is simply: long relative to what is normal or expected in that situation.
The Idea of Continuity Is Critical

The word is not just about age. It carries the sense that something has kept going without a significant break.

Consider this: if two countries had an agreement from 1900 to 1950, then it ended, and now it's 2026 — you would NOT call that a "longstanding agreement." It ended. It is a historical agreement, an old agreement, a past agreement — but not longstanding.

But if that agreement started in 1900 and is still in place today, then yes — it is absolutely a longstanding agreement.

This is what separates "longstanding" from simply "old." Something can be old but finished. Something longstanding is old and still continuing.
How It Is Used in a Sentence

"Longstanding" always works as an adjective — it describes a noun. It most commonly sits directly before the noun it describes:

  • "There is a longstanding tradition in our family of eating together on Sundays."
  • "The two neighbors finally resolved their longstanding dispute over the fence."
  • "She is a longstanding member of the committee."
  • "Poverty is a longstanding problem in many parts of the world."

It can also come after a linking verb (like "is" or "has been"), though this is less common:

  • "The disagreement between the two sides is longstanding."
  • "Their friendship is longstanding and deeply valued."

Both forms are correct.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Several words feel close to "longstanding," but each has a slightly different flavour:

Old — simply means something has existed for a long time. It says nothing about continuity or whether it still exists. "An old agreement" might be finished. "A longstanding agreement" is definitely still active.

Deep-rooted — means something is strongly embedded in a system, culture, or person — like the roots of a tree that go very deep. It emphasizes how hard something is to remove or change, not just how long it has been there. A longstanding tradition might be deep-rooted, but not always.

Persistent — means something keeps continuing, especially despite efforts to stop or fix it. It carries a slightly negative tone and focuses on the difficulty of ending something. A longstanding problem can be called persistent, but persistent focuses on the stubborn nature of it, while longstanding focuses on the duration.

Enduring — means something has lasted through challenges and time, and often carries a positive, admirable quality. "An enduring love" suggests beauty and resilience. Longstanding is more neutral — it simply states the fact of long duration without the admiring tone.

Established — means something is accepted, recognized, and in place. A longstanding institution is likely also established, but "established" focuses more on being officially set up and recognized, while "longstanding" focuses purely on how long it has been around.
A Quick Test to Know If You're Using It Correctly

Before using the word, ask yourself two questions:

  1. Did this thing begin a long time ago? ✅
  2. Is it still continuing (or was it still continuing at the point in time being discussed)? ✅

If both answers are yes, longstanding fits perfectly.

If the thing started recently → don't use it.
If the thing ended long ago → don't use it.

Longstanding = has existed for a long time AND is still continuing.

It is a neutral word — used for both good things (friendships, traditions, agreements) and bad things (problems, disputes, feuds). It tells you about time and continuity, not about quality or value. The "how long" is always relative to the situation, and the key detail that makes something truly longstanding is that it has not stopped — it is ongoing.
10117:
A longueur is a stretch or passage within a book, film, play, speech, or piece of music that feels tediously slow and dull — a section that drags on, loses your attention, and makes you feel like time is crawling. Think of it as a "dead spot" inside an otherwise larger work.

The key idea is that it doesn't describe the entire work as boring. It describes a specific section or period within something that, as a whole, might even be quite good.
What Makes It Different From Just Saying "Boring"?

This is important. Saying "the movie was boring" means the whole thing failed to hold your interest. But spotting a longueur is a more precise and surgical judgment — it means:

"This particular section dragged. It slowed things down unnecessarily. It made me restless and impatient. And it didn't need to be this long."

A seasoned film critic, for instance, might say: "The film is largely magnificent, but it suffers from longueurs in the second act." That tells you something very specific and useful — the film isn't bad overall, but there are particular stretches where it loses its energy and your attention starts to wander.

A longueur is not just about something taking a long time. It's about something feeling longer than it should — the dragging, restless feeling where you're glancing at the clock, flipping pages impatiently, or shifting in your seat. It's the subjective experience of time slowing down because the content isn't earning your attention.

This is a subtle but crucial point: a three-hour film can have zero longueurs if every scene crackles with energy. A thirty-minute speech can have painful longueurs if the speaker meanders, repeats themselves, or pads their points with unnecessary detail.
Where You'll See This Word Used

Longueur is almost exclusively used in critical or intellectual writing — book reviews, film criticism, literary essays, opera reviews, and cultural commentary. It's a word critics reach for when they want to say, with precision and elegance, that a work loses its momentum in places. You are far more likely to read it than to hear it in everyday conversation.

You will almost always see this word in the plural form: longueurs. This is because creative works rarely have just one problem patch — they tend to have several. So the typical usage sounds like:

  • "The novel has its longueurs, but the final hundred pages are extraordinary."
  • "Despite some longueurs in the middle section, the symphony builds to a breathtaking conclusion."

The singular longueur is valid but rarer, and you'd use it when pointing to one specific dragging moment:

  • "The trial scene is the one major longueur in an otherwise taut thriller."

1. "I loved the documentary, though there were a few longueurs whenever it shifted away from its central subject."
  2. "Even Shakespeare's greatest plays have longueurs that modern audiences find hard to sit through."
  3. "The speech was passionate, but the longueurs in the middle lost the crowd's attention."
A longueur is a tediously slow, dragging passage within a larger work — a section that outstays its welcome, saps your attention, and makes time feel heavier than it should.
10118:
To look at someone blankly means to stare at a person with absolutely no expression on your face — no smile, no frown, no raised eyebrow, nothing. Your face looks completely empty, like a blank sheet of paper with nothing written on it.

This empty look on your face is usually a signal of one of these things:

  • You didn't understand what the person just said.
  • You don't recognize who the person is.
  • You are so confused or shocked that your brain freezes and your face shows nothing.
  • You simply have no idea how to respond.

The whole meaning of this phrase lives in the word "blank."

Think of a blank page — it has nothing on it. No words, no pictures, no marks. Now imagine your face being like that blank page. When you look at someone blankly, your face is empty of any readable emotion or reaction. The word "blankly" is the adverb form of "blank," describing how you are looking — in a completely empty, expressionless way.

When someone looks at you blankly, you will notice:

  • Their eyes are open and fixed on you, but they seem to be "looking through you" rather than truly seeing you.
  • Their facial muscles are relaxed and still — no movement at all.
  • Their mouth is neither smiling nor frowning — it is simply neutral or slightly open.
  • They may blink slowly or stare without blinking.
  • They look almost like a person who is daydreaming or whose mind has suddenly gone empty.

It is as if the lights are on, but nobody is home.

This phrase is used in several different real-life situations. Understanding each one will make the idiom much clearer.

1. When someone doesn't understand you
This is the most common situation. You explain something — maybe a joke, a complex idea, or an instruction — and the other person has no idea what you just said. Their face shows zero comprehension. They look at you blankly because their brain hasn't processed your words yet.

She explained the math problem step by step, but the students just looked at her blankly.

2. When someone doesn't recognize you
You walk up to a person you know, say hello, and they stare at you with an empty expression because they have no memory of who you are. That empty stare is a blank look.

He smiled and waved, but she looked at him blankly — she had completely forgotten they had met before.

3. When someone is in shock or disbelief
Sometimes news or an event is so unexpected that a person's emotions are temporarily paralyzed. Their face can't decide what to show, so it shows nothing.

When they told him he had won the lottery, he just looked at them blankly for a full ten seconds.

4. When someone has nothing to say
A person might look at you blankly not because they're confused, but because they genuinely have no response to give. They are silent and expressionless.

She asked him why he had lied, and he just looked at her blankly.
The Tone and Feeling of This Phrase

This phrase is usually neutral to slightly negative in tone. It often signals a communication breakdown — one person said something and the other person couldn't process it. It can feel:

  • Awkward — because silence and a blank face after you speak feels uncomfortable.
  • Frustrating — for the speaker, because they feel their words had zero impact.
  • Humorous — in casual or light-hearted contexts, especially when the blank look is a reaction to something obvious or silly.
  • Sad or cold — when used between people who know each other, a blank look can feel distant or even hurtful.
Subtle but Important Detail: It's Not Rudeness by Default

It is important to understand that looking at someone blankly is usually not intentional or rude. It is an involuntary reaction — the person's face simply reflects the emptiness in their mind at that moment. They are not trying to ignore you or be cold. Their brain is genuinely stuck, confused, or processing something.

However, in some rare contexts, a person might deliberately give a blank look to express that they are unimpressed, bored, or dismissive. Context always tells you which meaning applies.
How It Compares to Similar Expressions

Knowing related expressions helps you understand the edges of this idiom's meaning.

  • "Look at someone blankly" = empty face, no expression, no understanding or recognition.
  • "Stare blankly" = almost the same, but "stare" emphasizes a longer, more fixed gaze. You can stare blankly at a wall too, not just a person.
  • "Give someone a blank stare" = the noun version of the same idea. "She gave him a blank stare."
  • "Look at someone with a puzzled expression" = this is different — a puzzled expression shows visible confusion (furrowed brows, squinting). A blank look shows no expression at all.
  • "Look at someone blankly" vs. "look at someone vacantly" = these are very close in meaning. "Vacantly" suggests the person's mind is completely elsewhere — like they are daydreaming. "Blankly" more often suggests confusion or failure to understand something specific.

Here are varied examples so you can see the phrase in action across different contexts:

  1. The teacher made a joke about history, but the young children just looked at her blankly.
  2. He said "good morning" to the new colleague, who looked at him blankly before realizing he was talking to her.
  3. I asked my grandfather if he remembered the film, and he looked at me blankly — he had never heard of it.
  4. When the doctor told her the diagnosis, she looked at him blankly, unable to process what she had just heard.
  5. My dog looked at me blankly when I asked him to sit — he clearly hadn't learned that command yet. (used humorously with animals)
  6. He looked at the exam question blankly — his mind had gone completely empty.
One-Line Summary to Remember It Forever

"Look at someone blankly" means to stare at a person with a completely empty, expressionless face — usually because you don't understand them, don't recognize them, or are too shocked to react.

Think of it this way: your face is a whiteboard, and at that moment, someone has erased everything on it.
10119: Lookout is about watching — specifically, watching carefully for something that might be coming, whether danger, opportunity, or anything else worth noticing. The word carries a sense of alertness and anticipation. Think of someone standing on a ship's mast, scanning the horizon. That image captures the spirit of every meaning below.
Meaning 1: A person whose job is to watch and warn

A lookout is a person assigned to keep watch — to observe the surroundings and alert others if something important appears, especially something dangerous.

This person doesn't fight or act; they watch and warn. Their whole job is to keep their eyes open so others don't have to.

Examples:

  • The gang posted a lookout at the end of the street to warn them if the police came.
  • During the robbery, one thief stayed outside as a lookout while the others went in.
  • The ship's lookout spotted the iceberg just in time to radio the captain.

You'll notice this meaning often appears in contexts involving secrecy, danger, or military/naval settings — situations where someone needs advance warning.
Meaning 2: The act or duty of watching carefully

Lookout can also refer to the activity of watching — the state of being alert and watchful. This meaning most commonly appears in the phrases "on the lookout" and "keep a lookout."

On the lookout means actively watching or searching for something — you're alert, aware, and expecting it might appear.

Examples:

  • Police are on the lookout for a white van seen near the crime scene.
  • She's always on the lookout for good deals at the market.
  • Keep a lookout for any spelling mistakes in the document.
  • The hikers kept a sharp lookout for snakes on the trail.

Notice that "on the lookout" doesn't have to mean danger — you can be on the lookout for something positive, like a job opportunity or a friend in a crowd. The key idea is active watchfulness.
Meaning 3: A place from which to watch

A lookout can be a physical location — usually a high or open spot — that gives a wide, clear view of the surrounding area. It's a place designed or used for watching.

Examples:

  • They climbed to the mountain lookout to watch the sunrise.
  • The forest ranger sat in the lookout tower, scanning for signs of fire.
  • The old coastal lookout post was built during the war to spot enemy ships.
  • From the lookout at the top of the hill, you could see the entire valley.

This meaning is very common in nature, tourism, and military contexts. You'll often see "lookout point," "lookout tower," or "lookout post."
Meaning 4: Someone's own problem or concern (chiefly British)

This meaning is more informal and mainly used in British English. When you say something is someone's lookout, you mean it's their responsibility, their problem to deal with — and often, that you're not going to worry about it for them.

Examples:

  • If he wants to quit his job without a plan, that's his own lookout.
  • You were warned about the risks. If it goes wrong, it's your lookout.
  • "Should I tell her?" — "That's entirely your lookout, not mine."

This usage carries a slightly detached tone — you're stepping back and saying, "this is your affair, your concern, your business to manage."

All four meanings flow naturally from the same root idea: watching out for what's ahead.

  • A person does it → a lookout (the watcher)
  • The act of doing it → on the lookout (the watching)
  • The place to do it from → a lookout (the observation point)
  • What you're responsible for watching over → your lookout (your concern)

ExpressionMeaning

"On the lookout" — actively watching or searching for something.
"She's on the lookout for a new apartment."

"Keep a lookout" — to watch carefully, usually for something specific.
"Keep a lookout for the turning — it's easy to miss."

"Sharp lookout" — watching with extra care and attention.
"The guards kept a sharp lookout through the night."

"That's your lookout" — that's your problem or responsibility (British English).
"If you miss the train, that's your lookout."
A note on tone and context

The word lookout often carries a slightly serious or alert tone — it implies that something matters and someone is paying attention. Even when used in casual speech ("keep a lookout for a parking spot"), there's a small sense of purpose and vigilance built into the word.

It is also worth knowing that "lookout" is sometimes spelled as two words — look out — but only when used as a verb or interjection ("Look out! A car!"). As a noun, it is always written as one word: lookout.
